shortLabel: Mendon town birth record: Samuel son of John & Ruth Gurney (14 March 1671)
statement: The Mendon, Massachusetts town book records the birth of a son to the John Gurney household: "Samuel son of John & Ruth Gurney — born March 14, 1671," the primary record fixing the wife's name Ruth and adding a third child, Samuel, to the household alongside John and Mary.

unit.title: Family — Mendon: John Jr. and Ruth Bundy

shortLabel: Plymouth/Taunton primary record: Ruth (Gurney) m. John Bundy, 9 Jan 1676
statement: The Plymouth Colony court's printed record of town returns and the Taunton town's own vital records both carry the 9 January 1676 marriage of John Bundy to a Ruth Gurney of Mendon, under the colonial spellings "Surney" and "Garney"; Charles Henry Pope's 1900 compilation independently records the same marriage but misnames the bride "Jane."

unit.title: Family — Mendon: John Jr. and Ruth Bundy

shortLabel: John Jr. and Ruth's Mendon household, 1671-1676
statement: John Gurney Jr., son of the emigrant John Gurney-1, had settled at Mendon by the early 1670s with his wife Ruth and children John, Samuel (b. 14 March 1671), and Mary. He was among the dead when Nipmuc forces struck Mendon on 14 July 1675, the opening bloodshed of King Philip's War, and Ruth remarried John Bundy of Taunton on 9 January 1676.

unit.title: Family — Mendon: John Jr. and Ruth Bundy

shortLabel: Which John died at Mendon in 1675: G13's son, not Richard G12's son
statement: The 1675 Mendon casualty is John Gurney Jr., son of the emigrant John Gurney-1 (G13), not the identically-named eldest son of his brother Richard Gurney (G12). Richard's own son John was still living on 27 October 1691, when he declined to administer his father's estate — a record that rules him out as the 1675 casualty and resolves a confusion that had attached the Mendon death to the wrong generation.

unit.title: Family — Mendon: John Jr. and Ruth Bundy

shortLabel: Mendon Proprietors' Records: John Gurny's 20-acre lot, sold 1692
statement: The Mendon proprietors' records list "John Gurny, a twenty acre lot" among the town's earliest purchasers, and trace the same lot's chain of title through recurring meadow and swamp-lot abuttal references to its sale, by deed of 3 May 1692, to Josiah Thayer.

unit.title: Family — Mendon: John Jr. and Ruth Bundy

shortLabel: Mendon Proprietors' Records: Grisel Gurney's separate 20-acre lot and will
statement: The Mendon proprietors' records list "Grisel Gurney, a twenty acre lot" as a separate purchaser from John Gurny, and carry a copy of her will, returned to the town through guardians in Chelmsford, in which "the Widdow Gurny that Was And Last of all Wife to the Abouesd John Burge" left her Mendon accommodation to her son Joseph Juell, with payments due Nathanil Juell, Mercy Juell, and Sherabiah Keby.

unit.title: Family — Mendon: John Jr. and Ruth Bundy

shortLabel: Two Gurney lot-holders at post-1667 Mendon: the son and the widow
statement: The post-1667 Mendon proprietors' records preserve two separate Gurney lot-holders of the same generation: John Gurny, matching the resident son John Jr., whose twenty-acre lot passed out of the family by sale in 1692; and Grisel Gurny, John Sr.'s widow, holding her own twenty-acre lot in her own right and willing it to her son by an earlier marriage, Joseph Juell. The two records track the family's already-established son-who-settled-there and widow-who-remarried-elsewhere lines, not a single household.

unit.title: Family — Mendon: John Jr. and Ruth Bundy

shortLabel: Bodge: Peter Gurney, Capt. Isaac Johnson's company, Dedham muster 1675
statement: George Madison Bodge's roll of King Philip's War soldiers lists "Peeter Gurnay" under Weymouth in Captain Isaac Johnson's company, mustered at Dedham on 10 December 1675 for the Narragansett campaign, and absent from that company's list of the Great Swamp Fight's December 1675 dead and wounded.

unit.title: Family — Mendon: John Jr. and Ruth Bundy

shortLabel: Peter's King Philip's War service and 1676 death
statement: Peter Gurney, John Gurney-1's youngest documented son, served as a soldier in Captain Isaac Johnson's company, surviving the Narragansett campaign's Great Swamp Fight of 19 December 1675, and was killed later in the war, in 1676.

unit.title: Family — Mendon: John Jr. and Ruth Bundy

shortLabel: Unresolved John-Jr.-line leads: the Nevis-will Mary and the Taunton Cooper marriage
statement: Two leads point past the John Jr./Ruth household without yet reaching it: whether the "Mary Gurney the daughter of John Gurney" named in the 1699 Nevis will of John Lewis (proved 1701) is John Jr.'s daughter and a granddaughter of G13 in the Lloyd New-England-and-Bristol merchant network; and whether the Elizabeth Gurney who married Timothy Cooper at Taunton on 16 October 1706 is a child or grandchild of John Jr. and Ruth carried into Ruth's Bundy household. Neither is yet confirmed by any connecting record.

shortLabel: 1695-96 Providence warning-out of John Gurney, a stranger
statement: Providence, Rhode Island's town council ordered a transient "John Gurney" to leave town on 31 March 1695; when he returned, the council in 1696 ordered him apprehended and fined 5 shillings or whipped twelve stripes and removed from town.

shortLabel: 1714 Providence will and inventory of Sarah Gurney; husband John Gurney alive
statement: Sarah Gurney of Providence died 16 April 1714; her will of 31 March 1714, proved 30 April 1714, names her husband John Gurney as still living — he witnessed the will and co-appraised the inventory by mark — and leaves everything to her children by a prior marriage, all surnamed Field.

shortLabel: The Providence John and Sarah Gurney household, 1695-1714: real but unconnected
statement: The Providence John and Sarah Gurney household — a stranger warned out of town in 1695-96 who by 1714 had married the widow Sarah Field and outlived her — is a genuine colonial-era same-surname couple with no record connecting either spouse to John Gurney-1's own children or grandchildren. All of Sarah's children carried her first husband's surname, Field, so the Gurney marriage left no recorded offspring of its own.

shortLabel: Torrey's John3 entries: a plausible but unconfirmed grandson reading
statement: Torrey's compendium independently carries the Providence couple ("John3 ... & Sarah (Thornton)[Fields] ... b 1714; Providence") alongside a second John3 married to Elizabeth Green at Weymouth in 1689 and a Samuel3 - probably, though not conclusively, John Gurney Jr.'s Mendon-born son (an identification tested, not asserted, in the family Mendon-descendants unit) - married in 1693. If that Samuel3 identification holds, the generational placement is consistent with, but does not prove, the Providence John being a grandson of John Gurney-1 through John Jr.'s Mendon household, while the separate Weymouth John3 more plausibly belongs to Richard G12's own Weymouth line. Torrey's entry states no parentage for either John3, and his "Thornton" reading is most plausibly a slip for Josiah Thornton, the 1714 inventory's co-appraiser, not a prior husband's surname.

shortLabel: Suffolk Deeds Liber I index: "Gurner, James, 5" (unread)
statement: Suffolk Deeds, Liber I's printed index (covering 1640-1653) carries the unexplained line "Gurner, James, 5," immediately beside "Gurdon, John, 5"; the body text on printed page 5 has not been read.

shortLabel: Open: identity of "James Gurner," Suffolk Deeds Liber I
statement: Whether "James Gurner" in Suffolk Deeds Liber I's index is a genuine Gurney-variant colonial datum — comparable to the Norwich-attested James Gurney, son of the laceweaver Francis — or a Garner/Gardner-type false friend of the kind resolved for colonial Dorchester remains unresolved; the printed page 5 body text needs to be read.

shortLabel: 1664 Margery Laver will: bequest "to Jane Gurnet"
statement: Margery Laver of Dorchester's will, dated 4 (6) 1664 and proved 10 (9) 1664, bequeaths 2 shillings "to Jane Gurnet, 2s for a memorandum," among legacies to Braintree's minister William Tompson, Dorchester's minister Richard Mather, and the Wiswall and Preston families.

shortLabel: The Gornell/Gurnell record stream: "Goodman Gurney of Dorchester" across three sources
statement: Dorchester's own town book renders one resident, John Gurnell, under a dozen colonial spellings — Gornell, Gornill, Gornehill, Gurnell, Gurnel, gornett, Gurnett, Gurnet, Gurnit — including "John Gurnet" in a 13 (12) 1653 fence-viewers list; the Suffolk County Court's 1676/7 Prise-case surety names "Goodman Gurney of Dorchester" for what is the same man; and First Church Dorchester's record of 11 May 1709 still calls his son's widow, Jane Gornell, "mrs. Burgesse alias Gurnet" when the church recovers a legacy she had left it.

shortLabel: Negative: no true Gurney household at colonial Dorchester
statement: No independent Gurney household existed at colonial Dorchester. Both the 1664 "Jane Gurnet" legacy and the 1676/7 "Goodman Gurney of Dorchester" surety resolve to the Gornell/Gurnell family under ordinary clerk-level spelling drift, confirmed across three independent Dorchester record streams; no Dorchester "Gurney" record should be read as evidence of John Gurney-1's family.

shortLabel: Candidate B: John was probably the son of Francis Gurney and Margaret Rybett
statement: John Gurney of Braintree was probably the son of Francis Gurney, a Merchant Taylor of West Barsham, Norwich and London, by his first wife Margaret Rybett, whom Francis married at Norwich on 23 September 1611. The identification rests on two primary records — that marriage and a degraded East Dereham baptism entry read as "John the sonne of ffrancis Gurnie" — supported by a father-to-son trade, an emigration corridor, a documented financial motive, and a Gurney kindred settled within five miles of the register. No record names John as Francis's son; the case is cumulative and indirect, and four offsets hold it below certainty.

shortLabel: Francis Gurney identified: sixth son of Henry Gurnay of Great Ellingham and West Barsham, b. 1581
statement: Francis Gurney was born 13 September 1581 at West Barsham Hall, Norfolk, the sixth son of Henry Gurnay, Esq., of Great Ellingham and West Barsham, by his wife Ellen Blennerhassett. Henry had twelve children; the family was old Norfolk gentry with an armigerous pedigree, and a sixth son had little to inherit.

shortLabel: Francis Gurney's Merchant Taylors' apprenticeship 1599–1605 and freedom, 30 June 1606
statement: Francis Gurney was bound apprentice in London on 14 May 1599, aged about seventeen, to Henry Tryme of the Merchant Taylors' Company "near Ludgate," for a seven-year term from Whitsun. On 3 February 1605 the Company court assigned him over to William Smooth, Merchant Taylor of Lothbury, ahead of a documented journey north. He was admitted to the freedom of the Company on 30 June 1606 (Daniel Gurney's Supplement gives 16 June, an unresolved two-week discrepancy).

shortLabel: Francis Gurney's Norwich commercial life and Lestrange agency, 1612–1636
statement: Daniel Gurney recorded that Francis Gurney's "commercial life began at Norwich," and the Hunstanton Hall account book of Sir Hamon Lestrange shows Francis acting as "a sort of agent, or banker" for the Lestranges, with payments running from January 1612 to May 1636. Thoms independently noted the frequent mentions of Francis Gurney the merchant in Alice Lady Lestrange's Hunstanton accounts.

shortLabel: Francis Gurney's failed King's Lynn worsted venture, 1622
statement: On 17 October 1622 Francis Gurney, citizen and merchant-taylor of London, agreed with Ambrose Tompson and Martin Hill to teach the poor children of King's Lynn to spin worsted yarn and to employ the borough's poor in that industry. The venture failed, and Sir Hamon Lestrange had to pay Francis's £100 bond.

shortLabel: Francis Gurney sells all his Norfolk and Suffolk lands, 11 July 1634
statement: By an indenture of 11 July 1634 between Fraunces Gurnay of London, Merchant Taylor, and Sir Owen Smith of Irmingland, Norfolk, Francis conveyed all his Norfolk and Suffolk manors and lands for £1,000 — a forced liquidation conducted through the Court of Wards.

shortLabel: Marriage of Francis Gurney and Margaret Rybett, St Martin at Palace, Norwich, 23 September 1611
statement: The register of St Martin at Palace, Norwich, records the marriage of "Franc Gurny & Margaret Rybett" on 23 September 1611. The entry was located in March 2026 in Norfolk Record Office PD 12/1 and the reading confirmed from the register image.

shortLabel: A first marriage unknown to the compilers, opening a family of the emigrant's generation
statement: Francis Gurney had a first wife before Anne Browning, and therefore a first family whose children fall about 1609–1617 — the generation the Massachusetts emigrant belongs to. The 1611 marriage also fills the otherwise unexplained thirteen-year gap between Francis's 1606 freedom and his first recorded child at St Benet Fink in 1619, and it confirms as fact the Pease genealogy's transmitted family tradition of a "Margaret Ryvett" first marriage. Neither Daniel Gurney nor Bernau ever found the record, so no child of that marriage could appear in their accounts.

shortLabel: The Rybett/Ryvett family, St Martin at Palace, and the corrected Heydon connection
statement: The Rybett or Ryvett family were Norfolk and Suffolk gentry, documented at Fritton in Norfolk and at Rishangles, Rattlesden, Stowmarket, and Bildeston in Suffolk. St Martin at Palace was their own Norwich parish, with Rivett entries running 1539–1603, so Margaret almost certainly married from her family's church. A reported marriage of Myrable Ryvett to Sir John Heydon is not borne out by the Visitation of Suffolk, which gives her husband as William Burd, Customer of London; the genuine Gurney–Heydon tie runs through Anne Heydon's marriage to William Gurney V. Francis Gurney was buried at St Botolph Bishopsgate, London, on 9 January 1646/7.

shortLabel: Margaret's Rivett kin at Garveston and Gressenhall, two to three miles from East Dereham
statement: Margaret Rybett is identifiable as Margaret Rivet, baptised 21 May 1586 at Garveston, Norfolk, daughter of Francis Rivet — a mid-Norfolk family, not the Suffolk gentry line. Garveston lies two miles from East Dereham and Gressenhall three, and the Rivett presence in both is continuous. This gives the long-standing hypothesis a documentary basis: John, left motherless about 1616–17 when Margaret died and Francis remarried and moved to London, had maternal kin a few miles from his birthplace. Richard Ryvett of Gressenhall, who married Faith in 1602, is a documented source for the name John gave his eldest surviving son.

shortLabel: Francis Gurney's East Dereham child cluster, c.1611–1633
statement: The East Dereham parish register (Norfolk Record Office, PD 86/41, 1593–1641) carries a cluster of Francis Gurney entries across 69 microfilm images: a baptism of Edward about 1611/12; a burial of a Marye in late 1615 or January 1616, whose relationship word does not read as "daughter" and who is likely a niece; the burial of Agnes, daughter of Francis Gurney, on 31 January 1616; the baptism of Marye, daughter of Francis Gurney, on 25 May 1618; and a probable burial of a son Francis on 8 November 1633. Many entries are too degraded for confident surname-sensitive reading and most dates carry a ±2-year margin where the page year is not visible.

shortLabel: Entry E, East Dereham image 00715: "John the sonne of ffrancis Gurnie," c.1609/10
statement: Entry E of the East Dereham register, on image 00715, was indexed by Findmypast and FreeREG as "John the sonne of Nicholas Gorne." Read under magnification against four confirmed "ffrancis Gurnie/Gurny" entries in the same register and the same hand, it reads instead as "John the sonne of ffrancis Gurnie," about 1609/10. Four independent letterform tests — the initial stroke cluster, the mid-body structure, the word segmentation, and the terminal formation — favour "ffrancis"; none favours "Nicholas."

shortLabel: Entry E is probably John Gurney-1's baptism
statement: Entry E is probably the baptism of John Gurney-1, making him the eldest known child of Francis Gurney by Margaret Rybett, born at East Dereham before the family moved to London. The reading is the strongest single link between the Massachusetts emigrant and the Norfolk Gurney line, and it is an inference from letterform comparison, not a legible entry.

shortLabel: Open: Entry E awaits professional examination of the original register
statement: The Entry E reading is an AI-assisted paleographic analysis, not a professional examination of the physical register. Professional examination of the original at the Norfolk Record Office, The Archive Centre, Martineau Lane, Norwich NR1 2DQ, is the canonical path to confirming or rejecting it, and has not been done.

shortLabel: The baptism date sits a year or two before the parents' marriage
statement: Entry E's estimated date of about 1609/10 may precede the 23 September 1611 marriage of Francis and Margaret by a year or two. Two readings absorb this: the register's ±2-year margin puts the entry within reach of the wedding, or John was born before his parents married, which was common enough in the period to pass without remark. Neither is forced, and the tension is real rather than fatal.

shortLabel: 1633 Heralds' Visitation: Francis attests Roger as his "eldest sonne"
statement: In the 1633 Heralds' Visitation of London, Francis Gurnay attested his own pedigree and children and named Roger as his "eldest sonne." Roger was baptised at St Benet Fink in December 1621. Taken as written, the attestation leaves no room for an older son, and it is the sharpest documentary objection to the Candidate B parentage.

shortLabel: The recorded child lists are not closed; the "eldest sonne" attestation does not exclude an older son
statement: Francis Gurney's recorded child list is demonstrably incomplete, so the 1633 "eldest sonne" attestation does not exclude an older son of the first marriage. Daniel Gurney called Dorothy the eldest child "mentioned in" the St Benet Fink register, judged Roger likely to have died young, and added beyond the register a son John of Maldon whom Francis "seems" to have had and a George who was "probably another son." Bernau warned outright that no complete record of the children of Francis and Anne Browning survives. Neither compiler knew of the 1611 marriage, and a visitation recorded the children a man presented, not all who existed.

shortLabel: No John among the seven St Benet Fink children of Francis and Anne Browning, 1619–1637
statement: No John appears among the seven children baptised to Francis Gurney and his second wife Anne at St Peter le Poer with St Benet Fink, London, 1619–1637: Dorithy (2 March 1619), Roger (20 December 1621), Frances (18 January 1625), Francis (13 November 1628), Lucretia (28 October 1630), Thomas (19 April 1636), and Margaret (28 July 1637). The silence supports rather than undercuts Candidate B: if John was Francis's son, he must belong to the first marriage, which is where the East Dereham entry places him.

shortLabel: Rye's two-Francis separation, anchored by the 1627 Parmentergate apprenticeship of James Gurney
statement: Walter Rye first separated two contemporary Francis Gurneys: the West Barsham gentleman and Merchant Taylor, at East Dereham c.1608–1618 and St Benet Fink 1619–1637; and a Norwich plebeian laceweaver of St Peter Mountergate, later of St Giles Cripplegate 1638–1640, wife Mary, to whom the Costessey property belongs. The Norwich corporate registers separate them by simultaneous independent record: James Gurney, son of a Francis of St Peter Parmentergate — the laceweaver's parish — was bound apprentice at Michaelmas 1627 for seven years and admitted a freeman of Norwich on 8 January 1648, while Francis the Merchant Taylor was baptising children at St Benet Fink in London in the same year. The same registers carry no John Gurney freedom or enrolled apprenticeship anywhere in the emigrant window.

shortLabel: 1640 St Giles Cripplegate burial: a third Francis Garney, joiner, and his infant John
statement: The St Giles Cripplegate register records the burial of "John sonne of ffrancis Garney Joyner" in December 1640; the child had been christened on 14 December and was buried on the 16th. The father's trade is joiner, not laceweaver, so this is a third London Francis Gurney/Garney, distinct from both the Merchant Taylor and the Norwich laceweaver. The infant John is not the emigrant.

shortLabel: The parentage claim attaches to Francis the Merchant Taylor, not to the two same-named contemporaries
statement: The Candidate B parentage attaches specifically to Francis Gurney the West Barsham gentleman and Merchant Taylor, and is protected against two same-named contemporaries — the Norwich laceweaver of St Peter Mountergate and Parmentergate, and a St Giles Cripplegate joiner. Keeping the three apart is what stops the argument from absorbing the wrong household's records, and it is the reason the Costessey property and the 1640 Cripplegate infant John belong to neither the emigrant nor his father.

shortLabel: Elizabeth (Gournay) Crowe of East Bilney, sister of the West Barsham heir, married before 20 Dec 1636
statement: Muskett's Suffolk Manorial Families prints a Crowe-of-East-Bilney pedigree naming a Gurney daughter no Gurney source recorded: "Bozoune Crowe, of E. Bilney; mar. before 20 Dec. 1636 = Elizabeth, dau. of Thomas, sister of Edward Gournay, of West Barsham, Esq." Elizabeth was therefore a daughter of Thomas Gurney III and Martha Lewkenor and a sister of the West Barsham heir Edward. East Bilney lies in Launditch hundred, about five miles from East Dereham.

shortLabel: Frances Hovell as Edward Gournay's widow, and "Cozen Gurney" in Mary Goodwin's 1647 will
statement: Two Hovell-of-Hillington pedigree charts in Muskett read "Frances Howell maried to Edward Gurney of East Basham in Com' Norf. Esqr." and "Frances, wife of Edward Gurney of East Barsham, co. Norfolk, Esq., 1647." The 1647 will of Mary Goodwin of St Giles', Norwich, widow — a Hovell by birth — names "Sister Byng: sister Frances Hovell of Hillington Cozen Gurney: cozen Coulson" among her legatees and was proved in the Archdeaconry of Norwich on 19 February 1647/8. Edward Gournay's widow was therefore Frances Hovell of Hillington, and the Hovells still acknowledged Gurney kin in November 1647.

shortLabel: The senior West Barsham branch in the East Dereham orbit, 1636–1641
statement: The senior West Barsham branch — under Candidate B, John's uncle's and cousins' household — was present in the East Dereham neighbourhood across exactly the years in question. Edward Gournay's sister Elizabeth kept house at East Bilney, five miles from East Dereham, from before December 1636; and when Edward died on 6 August 1641 his inquisition post mortem was taken at East Dereham on 13 October 1641. This does not name John or connect him to the branch. What it removes is the objection that a Gurney child baptised at East Dereham in 1609/10 would be a stranger to the parish.

shortLabel: Open: Bozoune Crowe's PCC will (PROB 11/289/177) is unimaged and may name Gournay kin
statement: Bozoune Crowe's will — made 15 September 1658 and proved 11 March 1658/9 — survives as PROB 11/289/177, catalogued at The National Archives under a misrendering of both names, "Will of Bozann Crome, Gentleman of East Bilney, Norfolk." It was found by a place-anchored catalogue probe after surname probes failed, and no image has been pulled. Whether it names his wife Elizabeth's Gournay kin is the one document that could convert the East Bilney geography into a stated kinship.

shortLabel: What the identification rests on, and the four offsets that hold it below certainty
statement: Four threads tie John to Francis's household and none is a document naming him a son: a trade that ran father to son but through no surviving indenture; the East Anglia-to-London corridor that sent roughly three in five Massachusetts Bay emigrants of the 1630s and under one in ten from London proper; the 1634 liquidation that left an adult elder son nothing to inherit; and the Gurney and Rivett kin in the parish. Four offsets hold the case below certainty: the 1652/3 deposition age of "50 or thereabouts" reads five to eight years older than Entry E; John named no child Francis; no English marriage or child baptism of his own has been found; and both formal trade-admission registers return documented negatives. What removes the remaining doubt is negative — every other documented English John Gurney of the period has been traced to a life that rules him out, including thirteen Prerogative Court probate records fixing seven distinct John Gurneys in England after 1637 — while Anderson's Great Migration Directory still records the origin as "Unknown," which no surviving record contradicts.

shortLabel: Candidate C: the eight-child Berkhamsted Gurney family, 1610-1636, and the absent Berkhamsted burial
statement: The Hertfordshire baptism index records eight children baptised at Berkhamsted to a father John Gurney between 1610 and 1636: Henry (1610), Sara (1615), Jhon (1624), Richard (1626), Elizabeth (1629), Michael (1631), Sarah (1634), and Francis (1636); the mother is not indexed. The Hertfordshire burial index records no John Gurney burial at Berkhamsted between 1640 and 1700, the only seventeenth-century Berkhamsted burials under the name being two entries for a Jhon Gourney, in 1612 and 1620, both too early to be this householder.

shortLabel: Candidate C (Berkhamsted) eliminated on age, child set, and child chronology
statement: Candidate C, the Berkhamsted John Gurney, is eliminated on three independent grounds. Henry's 1610 baptism puts the father's own birth no later than about 1585-1590, thirteen to eighteen years before the colonial John's c.1603. Three of the eight Berkhamsted children - Henry, Michael, and Francis - have no counterpart in the colonial family, and the colonial John's Mary and Peter have no counterpart at Berkhamsted. The three shared names miss on date: Berkhamsted's John Jr. was baptised in 1624 against the colonial John Jr.'s c.1633, Richard in 1626 against c.1630, Sarah in 1634 against c.1628. Any one ground would suffice. Candidate C is the last of the principal named alternatives to be cleared.

shortLabel: Eleven Gurney households in the London hearth-tax returns, 1662-1666
statement: The London hearth-tax returns of 1662-1666 record eleven strict Gurney or Gurny household entries across the City of London, Westminster, and inner Middlesex. Among them: Walter Gurney at Greene Dragon Court in St Margaret's Westminster, 1 hearth, 1664; William Gurny on the south side of Fleet Street in St Bride's, 7 hearths, 1666, returned empty; William Gurney at Cock and Key Alley in St Dunstan in the West, 3 hearths, 1666; and Ann Gurney at Two Crane Court in the same parish, 5 hearths, 1666. All post-date the colonial John's death; none is a candidate for him.

shortLabel: The unknown-corridor residual: eliminating named households does not clear the record's gaps
statement: Eliminating named households is not the same as clearing the record. The same-name sweeps found more than forty distinct John Gurney heads of household in England between 1600 and 1670, and English parish-register coverage for the period is patchy enough that others existed unrecorded. The 1662-1666 London hearth-tax cluster makes the point concrete: eleven Gurney households in London alone, none of them surfaced by any candidate search, because a search built around a name, a wife, and a child set cannot see a household the registers never entered. The identity case file expresses this same residual as its two unknown-corridor scenarios, and it is the principal reason the estimate for Candidate B sits in the sixties rather than the nineties.

shortLabel: Did John emigrate through the Gurdon-Winthrop Court of Wards network, or merely out of the same county?
statement: Whether John Gurney reached Massachusetts through the Gurdon-Winthrop Court of Wards patronage network, or simply left the same county in the same decade as thousands of others, is unresolved. The network evidence is real but attaches to the senior West Barsham branch, not to him: Brampton Gurdon's letter of 20 October 1627 shows the widowed "mrs. Gurny" presenting her son's wardship through Winthrop's own office, and Candidate B's John stands two steps from that line, a nephew of it through his father Francis. No record connects him to it. A documented patronage route would turn a plausible corridor into a mechanism. The test that would close the chain is a patron-side search of the Norwich diocesan institution books for a 1627-28 presentation to the West Barsham vicarage made by right of the Gurney wardship; it cannot identify the emigrant, but it would make the Gurdon-Winthrop connection citable fact rather than strong construction.

shortLabel: Anderson's "Boston" settlement attribution reads as a conflation with the 1636 Newgate apprentice
statement: Anderson's Great Migration Directory gives John Gurney's New England settlements as Boston and Braintree, but no Boston record names him. The attribution is most plausibly the same conflation that produced the American family tradition of an 1615 birth at Southwark: the 1636 runaway apprentice John Gurney - a distinct, younger man - was bound to John Newgate the feltmaker and lived in Newgate's Boston household, a servant's position that would generate neither a church admission nor a property record. A short unrecorded stay at Boston by the elder John before he appears at Weymouth in June 1641 remains possible; Boston lay under a day away and traded with Weymouth constantly. But transient lodging is invisible in principle, so the scenario can be neither tested nor used.

shortLabel: The identification is reached by elimination and circumstantial fit, and predicts its own thin record
statement: John Gurney's parentage is settled by elimination and circumstantial fit, not by a document: no record made in his lifetime names his father. Two things make this elimination stronger than most colonial origin attributions. Every rival was actively disproved rather than left unexamined - Candidate A by continuous English residence to 1653, Candidate C by a family of the wrong shape, Candidate D by a 1662 London hearth-tax entry made in the year the colonial John lay dying, the Earsham testator by dying in England in 1638, and the 1636 Newgate apprentice by mismatched family status and an unbendable chronology. And the colonial record shows exactly one adult Gurney household in Massachusetts before 1660: the Dorchester "Gurneys" are Gurnells, the Providence John and Sarah are a later unconnected pair, and there is no second emigrant John. The weakness mirrors the strength. Candidate B predicts a man who would leave almost no English paper - a motherless son raised by his mother's kin, trained outside both guild registers that would have recorded him - so the absence of a confirming document is what the hypothesis expects and cannot be counted against it.

shortLabel: Two realistic end-states for the estimate and three levers that would move it
statement: Two end-states are realistic for the parentage estimate. A marriage record for John and Mary in the Rivett-orbit parishes around East Dereham, or a kinsman's mention of a Gurney beyond the seas in one of the unread Norfolk family wills of the 1650s, would lift the identification from probable to highly probable, near eighty-five to ninety percent. Failing that, continued negative searching leaves it a permanently caveated best identification in the sixty-five to seventy percent band. Three levers carry most of the remaining value: Norfolk parish and probate images in the Rivett orbit, a professional examination of the East Dereham register, and a Y-DNA test of the discriminating English-line kit. The fact sheet now matches the case file's about-sixty-five-percent estimate; the figure remains a caveated synthesis of indirect evidence, not a substitute for the missing direct record.

shortLabel: Boston silence: every surviving Boston-era record class holds no John Gurney
statement: Anderson's Great Migration Directory assigns John Gurney a Boston settlement beside Braintree, but no Boston record of any class names him. An exhaustive sweep of every surviving Boston-era record class - First Church admissions and baptisms, the Book of Possessions and Boston town records, the Aspinwall notarial register, Lechford's note-book, Suffolk Deeds Libers I-III, and the Boston vital records 1630-1699 - returns no Gurney of John's generation, and a manuscript-level full-text search adds none. This converts the 'Boston' attribution from an inference-level qualification into a record-level negative: John's documented life belongs wholly to his four towns, and the attribution is best read as a conflation with the 1636 Newgate apprentice, a Boston household servant who would have generated neither a church admission nor a property record.

shortLabel: Negative: First Church Boston (CSM 39) records no Gurney, 1630-1778
statement: The Records of the First Church in Boston (CSM Publications 39) - the town's only church of the 1630s-1640s, its admissions, votes, and baptisms running 1630-1778 - contain no Gurney of any spelling, though John Newgate, the feltmaker in whose Boston household the 1636 apprentice John Gurney lived as a servant, was himself a member. The last Boston-side record class thus closes against Anderson's 'Boston' settlement attribution for the elder John.

shortLabel: Negative: Boston town, notarial, deed, and vital record classes hold no John-era Gurney
statement: The printed Boston-era civil record classes hold no Gurney of John Gurney's generation: the Book of Possessions and Boston town records, the Aspinwall notarial register of 1644-1651, Thomas Lechford's note-book of 1638-1641, the earliest Suffolk Deeds (Libers I-III, 1640-1660), and the Boston vital records 1630-1699 are each silent. The single Gurney in the Boston vital records is the 26 October 1693 marriage of Samuel Gurney and Sarah Shapley - probably John's grandson, an identification tested (not asserted) in the family Mendon-descendants unit - married thirty years after John's death, so no Boston civil record touches the emigrant himself.

shortLabel: Negative: FamilySearch full-text sweep surfaces no new John Gurney colony document
statement: A FamilySearch full-text search across the Massachusetts Bay colony-records films and the Massachusetts State Archives (Felt) colonial-period volumes surfaced no John Gurney document beyond the two already known (the 1641 gunpowder-fine calendar and the 1644 bill). The residual '+Braintree +meadowes' images resolve to the 1664 will of James Penniman and the 1689/90 will of Richard Brackett, neither naming a Gurney. Manuscript-level searching thus adds no record to the printed footprint.

shortLabel: Negative: Early Providence records hold no Gurney; bounds the Quinapaug interest
statement: The Early Records of the Town of Providence (town-meeting and probate volumes swept) hold no Gurney of any spelling; the only near-name is a distinct Thomas Garnet family of Providence. The 1655-1675 town and deed volumes are clean, which bounds John Gurney's unlocated 'Quinapaug' interest - a Providence-jurisdiction frontier share carried into his 1663 inventory - as one the Providence record never registered. (The separate 1690s Providence John-and-Sarah Gurney household sits in volumes outside this sweep and is unaffected.)

shortLabel: 1646 Braintree meadows petition (imaged; Mass. Archives vol. 45)
statement: In 1646 John Gurney was among the signers of a Braintree inhabitants' petition to the General Court against Thomas Gilbert's cattle grazing the petitioners' meadow lots; the imaged document (Massachusetts Archives vol. 45, p. 11, with the answer slip at p. 11a endorsed over Gov. John Winthrop) places John among the town's founding cohort — Martin Sanders, Peter and Richard Brackett, Henry Adams, Samuel Bass, Samuel Adams, Benjamin Albee, John Dassett, James Penniman, and Thomas Meakins.

shortLabel: Blomefield: the Gurney-held West Barsham living, its 1603-1743 institution gap, and the excluded Norfolk livings
statement: Blomefield's parish histories locate the 1627 presentation on the West Barsham side. At West Barsham (vol. vii, pp. 42-47) the Gurneys held the vicarage advowson - 'In 1603, Leonard Metcalf occurs vicar, and certified 420 communicants; patron then, Henry Gurney' (Henry G15) - and the printed vicars list records no institution between 1603 and 1743, so a c.1627-28 presentation of Warford there is invisible in Blomefield; a competing Fermor advowson interest is also on record (William Fermor lord 'with the advowson' in 1627). The two other Gurney-associated Norfolk livings are excluded for 1627: Harpley (vol. viii, pp. 452-459) was held 1620-1648 by Edmund Gurnay B.D. under Sir William Yelverton, its advowson long out of the family, and Great Ellingham's one institution in the window (7 Nov 1628) was an Earl of Sussex presentation. West Barsham - where the heir Edward was in ward - is therefore the leading candidate for the presentation, with the Crown the likely patron of record during the minority whoever held the advowson in fee.

shortLabel: Adam Winthrop's diary records the 1605 deaths of Martha (Lewkenor) Gurney's Denham parents
statement: Adam Winthrop - John Winthrop's father - recorded in his diary the deaths of Sir Edward Lewkenor of Denham and his wife on 3 October 1605: 'Sir Edwarde Lewkenor of Denham in Suff[olk] Knight died of the smalpocks. Vir bonus et doctus fuit et patriae amans. The lady his wife died 2 dayes before him.' The couple were Sir Edward Lewkenor (d. 1605) and Susan (Heigham), the parents of Martha (Lewkenor) Gurney - so the Winthrop family personally memorialised the widowed Mrs. Gurney's own parents, in warm terms, a generation before the 1627 Gurdon-Winthrop letter carried a Gurney suit to John Winthrop's chamber.

shortLabel: The jest-book's West Barsham Gurney anecdotes are kin-sourced through the L'Estrange-Lewkenor marriage
statement: The Gurney anecdotes in Sir Nicholas L'Estrange's manuscript jest-book - printed in Thoms's 1839 Anecdotes and Traditions and long treated as detached hearsay - are kin-sourced family testimony. Muskett records that Sir Nicholas L'Estrange, 1st Bt. of Hunstanton (d. 1655), the jest-book's compiler, married Anne Lewkenor of Denham, daughter of Sir Edward Lewkenor II and so niece of Martha (Lewkenor) Gurney and first cousin of Edward Gournay of West Barsham. The compiler's own wife was therefore first cousin to the heir the anecdotes describe, moving them from hearsay to family testimony. The upgrade cuts both ways: it explains 'Frances Hood' as the jest-book's rendering of Edward's wife Frances Hovell, but it also shows that the mistaken 'died in 1614' - which the wills instead place at 1621x1623, the 1614 date belonging to Henry G15's revoked earlier will - was already circulating inside the family.

shortLabel: Thomas Chaplin's 1672 Bury will: 40 pounds to 'Mary Gurney my servant' beside a New England (Houchin) debt
statement: Thomas Chaplin of Bury St Edmunds, gent., 'being aged,' in his will dated 24 April 1672 (proved 25 November 1672, Archdeaconry of Sudbury) left 40 pounds 'to Mary Gurney my servant' - an extraordinary legacy for a servant, eight times the 5 pounds he left his own daughter Abigail Whiteing - and in the same will directed that a debt owing from 'Jeremy Houchin, late in New England' be collected and 60 pounds of it divided among his Shepherd grandchildren. The will places a Bury St Edmunds Gurney woman in service in 1672, in a household directly tied to Boston through the Houchin debt - a concrete instance of the Bury/New England traffic Banks's attribution gestured at. It names no John Gurney and connects to no identified natal household; its bearing is on the Suffolk-migration milieu, not on the emigrant's parentage.

shortLabel: Ann Gurney x John Gilman, Hingham Norfolk 1626
statement: Ann Gurney married John Gilman, a worsted weaver, at Hingham, Norfolk, on 1 October 1626; the couple's children were baptised at West Dereham and Hingham, Ann was buried at Hingham on 23 November 1651, and their son John Gilman Jr. later emigrated to Exeter, New Hampshire. West Dereham, in western Norfolk near Downham Market, lies about twenty miles from the East Dereham parish of Francis Gurney's children.

shortLabel: Was Ann Gurney (Gilman) John's sister?
statement: Whether the Ann Gurney who married John Gilman at Hingham in 1626 was John Gurney's sister is unresolved. The Pease genealogy identifies her as a daughter of Francis Gurney by his first marriage - which, if correct, would make her John's sister - but no primary record links her to Francis, her Gilman children were baptised at West Dereham some twenty miles from Francis's East Dereham parish, and a separately recorded Ann Gurney married Peter Woodcocke at West Dereham in 1618/19 and may be a different woman. The kinship rests on a single compiled genealogy, not a record.

shortLabel: Ann/Gilman as a Gurney instance on the Norfolk corridor
statement: The Ann Gurney x John Gilman marriage threads a Gurney-surname connection through the same Norfolk-to-New-England corridor that received John. It took place at Hingham, Norfolk - ancient Gurney manorial territory (the manor of Hingham Gurneys) and one of the parishes that fed the Norfolk cohort settling Hingham, Massachusetts - into a Norfolk worsted-weaving family, and the couple's son emigrated to New England. Whether or not Ann was John's own sister (an open question), the connection is a concrete Gurney instance on the corridor; if the sisterhood holds, it places a second Gurney sibling on the Norfolk-to-New-England route, reinforcing the corridor reading of a Norfolk origin. The origin conclusion itself is held to the identity work.

shortLabel: The Peter naming gap points to Mary's kin, not the Gurney line
statement: Of twelve indexed Peter-Gurney baptisms across Britain in the 1632–1642 window, none was fathered by a John Gurney, so the name Peter did not reach John's youngest son through any indexed Gurney parallel. Peter is not absolutely absent from Norfolk Gurney households — a Peter Gurney, son of Peter, was christened at Smallburgh in February 1641 — but it enters John's own branch most plausibly through his wife Mary's kin, where a Peter would sit unremarked. The name is therefore a pointer to Mary's family rather than to Francis, and is neither for nor against the Candidate B parentage; recovering Mary's surname would explain it independently of John's paternity.

shortLabel: John named no child Francis — the strongest naming-pattern argument against Candidate B
statement: John Gurney named no child Francis. In a period when a first or early son was routinely named for the father, that absence is the single strongest naming-pattern argument against the Candidate B parentage, and it stands as written: John's roster is Sarah, Mary, Richard, John Jr., and Peter, with no Francis among them. Four explanations have been offered — estrangement from a father who had lost everything, avoidance of a name attached to that ruin, maternal naming priority (Richard may honour Mary's kinsman Richard Ryvett of Gressenhall), or an earlier Francis who died young and left no record — but each is an undocumented hypothesis, not evidence. The absence qualifies the parentage hypothesis without refuting it.

shortLabel: No indexed English parish cluster matches the colonial John's full family signature
statement: No indexed English parish-register cluster matches the colonial John's full family signature — a John Gurney with a wife Mary and children Sarah, Mary, Richard, John Jr., and Peter — in the target window of roughly 1620–1640, across more than twenty Gurney-surname baptisms reviewed in the FamilySearch, Findmypast, and Ancestry indexed collections. The closest clusters are the candidate parishes already weighed (Berkhamsted, Aylesbury, Hitcham, Eythorne, Toddington, Ackworth), each weak on the children's dates, the mother's name, or both. The absence is best read as a coverage gap in the surviving and indexed registers — the first three children most plausibly lie in an unindexed eastern-England set — not as evidence that the children were born outside England, and least of all in Massachusetts. It is the baptism-register counterpart of the unrecovered English marriage, and it is the thin paper trail Candidate B predicts for a family raised outside the recording parishes.

shortLabel: The Brackett brothers' compiled Sudbury origin sits inside Gurdon's own patronage geography
statement: John's tightest documented Braintree associates, brothers Richard and Peter Brackett, are read by modern compiled genealogy as sons of a Sudbury, Suffolk family, Richard baptised at St Gregory, Sudbury, 16 September 1610 - Sudbury being Brampton Gurdon of Assington's own parliamentary borough (Gurdon's family held Assington, four miles away, from 1556; his father sat for Sudbury in 1571; Gurdon himself was elected its MP in January 1621) and the same Gurdon who brokered the 1627 wardship letter carrying the senior West Barsham Gurneys into Winthrop's Court of Wards circle. If the compiled Sudbury reading holds, John's closest colonial associates were themselves raised inside Gurdon's own patronage geography. This is a network suggestion at compiled level, not a documented tie: the 1907 Brackett Genealogy found no Sudbury connection at all, offering only a distinct, self-described 'meager' Norfolk (Wreningham) scrap instead, and neither the Sudbury baptism nor the Wreningham scrap has been checked against a parish-register image. It connects John to nothing by blood or record - only that his own documented associates sit, on the modern compiled reading, inside the same East Anglian puritan-gentry patronage web already documented for the senior branch.

shortLabel: 26 Oct 1693 Boston marriage: Samuel Gurney x Sarah Shapley
statement: Samuel Gurney married Sarah Shapley at Boston on 26 October 1693, per the printed Boston vital records (Ninth Report of the Record Commissioners, p. 210) - the only Gurney entry of any generation in the volume.

unit.title: Family — Mendon: John Jr. and Ruth Bundy

shortLabel: Is the 1693 Samuel Gurney John Jr. and Ruth's Mendon-born son?
statement: Whether the Samuel Gurney who married Sarah Shapley at Boston in 1693 is John Jr. and Ruth's Mendon-born son (b. 14 March 1671) is unresolved. No record names either Samuel's father. The identification is chronologically clean - a Samuel born in 1671 would have been twenty-two in 1693, an ordinary marrying age - and no other Samuel Gurney appears anywhere in the surviving colonial-era record to compete for it, but age and the absence of a rival are not the same as a document naming the connection outright. The identification is probable, not proven.

unit.title: Family — Mendon: John Jr. and Ruth Bundy

statement: The London port-emigration lists and the livery-company registers, searched for John Gurney's crossing and trade, return no emigrant John Gurney. Hotten's Original Lists (behind them TNA E 157/20) hold no Gurney passenger in any spelling; a ROLLCO all-company livery sweep finds no East-Anglian Gurney apprentice, the sole provincial tailoring-Gurney being the eliminated Buckinghamshire Candidate-A family.

The English probate courts and Norfolk parish/marriage indexes, searched for any record naming the emigrant, his father Francis, or his family, return no positive match. No Francis Gurney G14 will survives in the Commissary, Archdeaconry, Prerogative, or Norwich courts; the two Rattlesden Rivett wills name no Margaret and no Gurney; and the Norfolk parish and same-name indexes yield no John-son-of-Francis baptism and no matching household for John or his wife Mary.
